question: Under Wisconsin DNR rules, what personal flotation device (PFD) must every vessel -- including canoes, kayaks, and paddleboards -- carry?
choice_a: No PFD is required on non-motorized craft
choice_b: A cushion-style PFD only, of any brand
choice_c: At least one U.S. Coast Guard-approved wearable life jacket for each person on board
choice_d: One life jacket for the entire boat regardless of the number of people aboard
explanation: Wisconsin DNR requires every vessel, including canoes, kayaks, and paddleboards, to carry at least one USCG-approved wearable life jacket for each person aboard.
source_note: Wisconsin DNR Life Jacket Safety guidance (dnr.wisconsin.gov/Topic/Boat/LifeJackets)

question: In addition to a wearable life jacket per person, what additional PFD must a Wisconsin vessel 16 feet or longer carry?
choice_a: A second wearable life jacket for every passenger
choice_c: No additional device is required regardless of length
choice_d: One U.S. Coast Guard-approved throwable flotation device that is immediately accessible
explanation: Vessels 16 feet or longer must carry, in addition to a wearable PFD for each person, at least one USCG-approved throwable device (like a ring buoy or buoyant cushion) that is immediately accessible for a rescue.
source_note: Wisconsin DNR Life Jacket Safety guidance (dnr.wisconsin.gov/Topic/Boat/LifeJackets)

question: What life jacket rule applies specifically to a person operating a personal watercraft (PWC) in Wisconsin?
choice_a: The operator must wear a USCG-approved life jacket at all times the PWC is in use
choice_b: A life jacket only needs to be stowed on board, not worn
choice_c: Life jackets are optional for PWC operators over age 18
choice_d: Only passengers, not the operator, must wear a life jacket
explanation: Every person operating a PWC in Wisconsin is required to wear a USCG-approved life jacket the entire time the PWC is in use -- it is not sufficient to simply carry one on board.
source_note: Wisconsin DNR Life Jacket Safety guidance (dnr.wisconsin.gov/Topic/Boat/LifeJackets)

question: According to Wisconsin DNR guidance, federal law requires children under what age to wear a USCG-approved life jacket while underway in an open vessel on federally controlled waters?
explanation: DNR guidance notes that federal law requires children under age 13 to wear a USCG-approved life jacket while underway in an open vessel on federally controlled waters.
source_note: Wisconsin DNR Life Jacket Safety guidance (dnr.wisconsin.gov/Topic/Boat/LifeJackets)

question: Which watercraft are exempted from Wisconsin's life jacket carriage requirement, though DNR still encourages wearing one?
explanation: Sailboards and windsurfers are exempt from the life jacket carriage requirement under DNR guidance, though the state still encourages wearing one for safety.
source_note: Wisconsin DNR Life Jacket Safety guidance (dnr.wisconsin.gov/Topic/Boat/LifeJackets)

question: According to Wisconsin DNR's own safety messaging, what proportion of boating drowning fatalities involve victims who were not wearing a life jacket?
explanation: The Wisconsin DNR's boating safety overview states that more than 90% of boating fatalities related to drowning involve victims who were not wearing a life jacket, which is why DNR recommends everyone wear one at all times on the water.

question: How should an inflatable life jacket be maintained, according to standard manufacturer and boater-education guidance also reflected in Wisconsin's course material?
choice_a: Test it periodically to confirm it inflates and holds air for 16-24 hours, and inspect the cartridge for damage or corrosion
choice_b: It never needs inspection once purchased
choice_c: It should be stored fully inflated at all times
choice_d: Only the outer fabric needs to be checked; the inflation mechanism is maintenance-free
explanation: Inflatable life jackets require periodic testing to confirm they inflate properly and hold air for 16 to 24 hours, plus inspection of the CO2 cartridge for damage or corrosion, since a compromised cartridge won't inflate the jacket when needed.
source_note: Wisconsin DNR Life Jacket Safety guidance (dnr.wisconsin.gov/Topic/Boat/LifeJackets)

question: Why do boater education courses stress that a life jacket only works if it is actually worn?
choice_a: Life jackets are equally effective whether worn or stowed
choice_b: Because in an emergency there is often no time to put one on, and stowed jackets can be knocked out of reach when a person is thrown from the boat
choice_c: Because Wisconsin law only requires wearing one when swimming, not boating
choice_d: A stowed life jacket automatically inflates when the boat capsizes
explanation: Most boating accidents happen suddenly, leaving no time to locate and put on a life jacket that is merely stowed -- this is the core reasoning behind DNR's recommendation to wear one at all times.
source_note: Wisconsin DNR Boating Safety Overview and NASBLA-aligned curriculum, Unit 4: PFDs

question: What is the difference between a wearable PFD and a throwable PFD?
choice_a: A throwable PFD must always be worn, never thrown
choice_b: A wearable PFD can only be used by children
choice_c: A wearable PFD is worn on the body for continuous protection; a throwable PFD (like a ring buoy or cushion) is tossed to a person already in the water
choice_d: There is no functional difference between the two
explanation: A wearable PFD is designed to be worn continuously for protection if you go overboard, while a throwable device is meant to be thrown to someone already in the water to help keep them afloat -- Wisconsin requires the former for everyone aboard and the latter as backup on vessels 16 feet or longer.
source_note: Wisconsin DNR Life Jacket Safety guidance; NASBLA-aligned curriculum, Unit 4: PFDs

question: Why must a PFD fit properly to work as intended?
choice_a: Fit only affects comfort, not performance
choice_b: All PFDs are one-size-fits-all by federal design
choice_c: A loose PFD provides more buoyancy than a snug one
choice_d: A poorly fitted PFD can slip off or fail to keep the wearer's head above water, especially for children who need a properly sized child PFD rather than an adult size
explanation: A PFD that is too large can ride up or slip off in the water, so children and smaller adults need correctly sized PFDs -- a properly fitted PFD stays in place and keeps the wearer's head above water.
source_note: NASBLA-aligned boater education curriculum, Unit 4: PFDs

question: On Wisconsin's federally controlled waters, does an adult passenger who cannot swim have any different life-jacket obligation than an adult who can swim?
choice_a: No -- the wear requirement discussed by DNR is age-based (children under 13), not tied to swimming ability, though DNR recommends anyone who cannot swim well always wear one
choice_b: Non-swimmers are legally exempt from ever wearing a PFD
choice_c: Only non-swimmers are required to wear PFDs; swimmers never are
choice_d: Swimming ability changes the required PFD type from Type II to Type V
explanation: The specific wear mandate DNR highlights is age-based (children under 13 on open vessels on federally controlled waters); it does not carve out a different rule by swimming ability, though common-sense safety guidance still encourages weak or non-swimmers to wear a PFD at all times.
source_note: Wisconsin DNR Life Jacket Safety guidance (dnr.wisconsin.gov/Topic/Boat/LifeJackets)

question: What should a boater check for on a PFD before each outing?
choice_a: Only whether it is the current model year
choice_b: Rips, tears, waterlogging, mildew, broken straps or buckles, and overall USCG approval label condition
choice_c: Only the color of the fabric
choice_d: Nothing -- PFDs never degrade over time
explanation: A pre-trip PFD check should look for rips, tears, waterlogged or matted flotation material, mildew, and broken straps or buckles -- any of which can compromise the device's ability to keep a person afloat.
source_note: NASBLA-aligned boater education curriculum, Unit 4: PFDs
